books.section: Topic 6.9 Responses to Immigration in the Gilded Age

primary_sources: Henry Cabot Lodge, “The Restriction of Immigration,” North American Review, January 1891

stimulus.text:
“Thus it is proved, first, that immigration to this country is increasing, and, second, that it is making its greatest relative increase from races most alien to the body of the American people and from the lowest and most illiterate classes among those races. In other words, it is apparent that, while our immigration is increasing, it is showing at the same time a marked tendency to deteriorate in character.”

Henry Cabot Lodge, “The Restriction of Immigration,” North American Review, January 1891.
stimulus.source_note: Henry Cabot Lodge, “The Restriction of Immigration,” North American Review, vol. 152 (January 1891), p. 32, as reprinted in Publications of the Immigration Restriction League, No. 1 (1894). Public domain; text checked against the Internet Archive scan of the League’s Publications.

stem: Lodge’s argument was used to support which of the following proposals?

options.text: Opening Ellis Island to process arrivals faster
options.misconception: Names a faster welcome, the opposite of restriction.

options.text: A literacy test to keep out immigrants he judged undesirable
A law giving immigrants free farmland in the West
options.misconception: Names a gift of land, the opposite of keeping people out.

options.text: A treaty bringing more workers from China
options.misconception: Names bringing more workers in, the opposite of restriction.

rationales.A: Ellis Island, opened in 1892, processed arrivals. Lodge wanted to keep many of them out, not process them faster.
rationales.B: Lodge called the new immigration illiterate and deteriorating in character, and he proposed a reading test as the remedy. Background from the books: his literacy-test bill asked immigrants to read twenty words of the Constitution, and the Immigration Restriction League carried the same demand.
rationales.C: Free farmland would bring more immigrants in. Lodge wanted fewer, not more.
rationales.D: A treaty bringing Chinese workers would reopen the door the Exclusion Act had shut. Lodge wanted the door shut tighter.
rationales.general:
Match the complaint to the remedy it calls for.
1. Lodge complains the new immigrants are illiterate and deteriorating in character.
2. A reading test answers an illiteracy complaint directly.
3. Background from the books: Lodge's bill required reading twenty words of the Constitution.
4. Faster processing, free land, and more workers all answer the opposite complaint.
Remember: a proposal is the remedy for the complaint that comes just before it.
